pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 11–12 years

- **Topic:** Atoms, Elements & Compounds

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS3 Chemistry 'Atoms, elements and compounds'):** A simple (Dalton) atomic model; the differences between atoms, elements and compounds; chemical symbols and formulae for elements and compounds. (The sub-atomic structure — nucleus of protons and neutrons with electrons in shells — is commonly introduced at KS3 and formalised at GCSE/KS4.)

- **Standards — US (NGSS MS-PS1-1):** [curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-PS1-1].

- **Operational details:** The organising distinction is a hierarchy: atoms are the building blocks; an ELEMENT is one kind of atom; a COMPOUND is two or more kinds chemically joined in fixed ratio; a MIXTURE is substances together but not joined. Teach with models the child assembles — snap identical atoms to make an element, different atoms to make a compound, and read the formula off (H2O = two hydrogen + one oxygen). Introduce the simple atomic picture (a tiny central nucleus with electrons around it) to give atoms internal structure, and chemical symbols as the shorthand. The critical conceptual move: a compound has DIFFERENT properties from its elements (sodium + chlorine, both dangerous, make edible salt) and cannot be separated physically — unlike a mixture. Keep sub-atomic detail light (shells/electron arrangement is deepened at KS4).

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B–C (early-formal). The child classifies a given particle diagram/formula as element, compound or mixture, writes/reads a simple formula, and explains that a compound's properties differ from the elements that formed it.
bestPractices: Build the element/compound/mixture distinction by assembling atoms into models rather than defining the terms verbally.
Read formulae directly off built models so symbols and subscripts mean 'how many of each atom'.
Make the key move that a compound has NEW properties unlike its elements (Na + Cl2 → edible salt).
Contrast a compound (chemically joined, fixed ratio, not physically separable) with a mixture (just together, separable).
Keep sub-atomic detail light at KS3 (nucleus + electrons); defer electron shells/arrangement to KS4.
keyRepresentations: Atom-snap models for element, compound and mixture
Live chemical formula readout (e.g. H2O) tied to the model
A simple atom diagram (nucleus + surrounding electrons + symbol)
A 'try to separate' test distinguishing mixture (separable) from compound (not)
commonMisconceptions: A compound is just a mixture of its elements and keeps their properties.
A compound can be separated into its elements by physical means (filtering, etc.).
The subscript in a formula multiplies the whole formula rather than the preceding atom.
Elements and atoms are the same thing (confusing the substance with its building block).
A molecule of an element (e.g. O2) must be a compound because it has two atoms.

learn.summary: Learners build the atom 	a2192 element 	a2192 compound 	a2192 mixture hierarchy by assembling atoms rather than memorising definitions. The core conceptual moves: an element is one kind of atom; a compound is two or more kinds chemically joined in a fixed ratio and has NEW properties unlike its elements; a mixture is substances together but physically separable. Learners also read simple formulae as 'how many of each atom', match chemical symbols, and meet a light introduction to atomic structure: a central nucleus containing protons and neutrons with electrons in shells around it. Detailed electron-shell arrangement is kept light at this stage.

activities.title: Atom workshop: build and classify
feedback: If a learner labels a two-atom element molecule (e.g. O2) a compound, point out both atoms are the SAME kind 	a2014 it is still an element; a compound needs different kinds of atoms.
If a learner reads the subscript in H2O as doubling the whole formula, clarify the subscript counts only the atom it immediately follows: H2O is 2 hydrogen atoms and 1 oxygen atom.

If a learner expects to physically separate a compound, show the 'try to separate' test refusing the compound while cleanly splitting the mixture, and note a compound needs a chemical change to break apart, whereas a mixture separates by physical means.
activities.rationale: Constructing and classifying particles turns the hierarchy into an action rather than a verbal definition, and directly engages the common confusion between compounds and mixtures. A live formula readout and symbol key tie the shorthand to what was built. Interactive snapping, live formula updates and a separability test are illustrative mechanisms, not the only way to teach this; equivalent construction with physical atom models or paper cut-outs can serve the same purpose.
sourceClaims: DfE KS3 Chemistry: simple (Dalton) atomic model; differences between atoms, elements and compounds; chemical symbols and formulae
NGSS MS-PS1-1: [curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-PS1-1]
Students confuse compounds with mixtures and expect a compound to retain its elements' properties; building and testing separability targets this
learnerActions: Drag atoms from a palette and snap identical atoms together (e.g. two blue atoms) 	a2014 observe the classifier label the result 'element'.
Snap different atoms together (e.g. two blue + one red) and watch a formula box write the compound's formula while the classifier flips to 'compound'.

Scatter a jumble of two or more DIFFERENT kinds of separate particles that are not joined to each other (e.g. some blue–blue molecules alongside some separate red atoms) and observe the classifier read 'mixture'; note that a jumble of identical molecules is still one pure substance, not a mixture.
Use a 'try to separate' tool: pull a mixture cleanly into its parts, then try the same on a compound and find it cannot be pulled apart physically.
State in your own words why the built thing is an element, a compound, or a mixture, and read the formula off your model as a count of each kind of atom.
activities.intendedInsight: Element, compound and mixture are distinguished by how atoms are arranged: one kind of atom (element), different kinds chemically joined in a fixed ratio (compound), or substances merely together and separable (mixture). A formula records how many of each atom are joined.

activities.title: New properties: a compound is not its elements
feedback: If a learner predicts the magnet still pulls iron from iron sulfide, that signals treating the compound as a mixture 	a2014 the pre-observation reasoning is the key diagnostic; reteach compound vs mixture at the particle level.

If a learner says water should help things burn 'because oxygen is in it', contrast with salt: sodium reacts violently in water and chlorine is poisonous, yet salt is edible 	a2014 bonding creates new properties. Likewise, the oxygen in water is chemically joined to hydrogen, so water does not behave like oxygen gas and does not support burning; it is often used to put out ordinary fires (though not every fire, e.g. oil or burning-metal fires).
Full understanding: 'a compound's properties are new, unlike a mixture where each part keeps its own.'
activities.rationale: A predict-observe-explain contrast (iron+sulfur mixture vs iron sulfide compound) and the sodium+chlorine	a2192salt case make the 'new properties' move concrete and target the classic misconception that a compound keeps its elements' properties. The reasoning before observation is what reveals the misconception.
sourceClaims: Students confuse compounds with mixtures and expect a compound to retain its elements' properties; building and testing separability targets this
learnerActions: Compare the properties of reactive sodium metal and poisonous chlorine gas, then observe (via demonstration or described reaction) that combined they form ordinary edible table salt (NaCl).
State what changed: the compound has its OWN properties, different from both elements.
Predict for iron filings mixed with sulfur powder: can a magnet still pull out the iron, and does it still look like iron + sulfur? (Yes 	a2014 it is a mixture; each part keeps its own properties.)

Then consider a fresh portion heated to form dark grey iron sulfide and predict whether the magnet still pulls out iron (No, if all the iron has reacted: a new compound has formed. In real demonstrations leftover unreacted iron may still be attracted, so any pull comes from leftover iron, not from the compound).
Explain the difference between the two iron/sulfur results in terms of 'just together' versus 'chemically joined'.
activities.intendedInsight: When elements chemically combine into a compound, the compound has genuinely new properties, unlike a mixture where each component keeps its own properties and can be separated physically.

activities.title: Atom structure and symbol reference
feedback: If a learner confuses 'atom' and 'element', clarify an element is a substance made of ONE kind of atom (many of them), while an atom is the single building block.
When reading CO2, confirm 1 carbon atom and 2 oxygen atoms, and that it is a compound because it contains different kinds of atoms.
Reinforce reading the subscript as the count of the preceding atom only.
activities.rationale: A reference/vocabulary anchor supports the structure and symbol targets named in the objective (nucleus with protons/neutrons, electrons in shells). A fixed diagram and symbol key cannot let a learner build formulae or test separability, so this activity is best paired with the building activities rather than used alone. Keep detailed electron-shell arrangement light at this stage; it is deepened later.
sourceClaims: DfE KS3 Chemistry: simple (Dalton) atomic model; differences between atoms, elements and compounds; chemical symbols and formulae
learnerActions: Explore a labelled atom diagram showing a tiny central nucleus 	a2014 containing protons and neutrons 	a2014 with electrons arranged around it in shells, together with the element's chemical symbol (the electron-shell detail is kept light at this stage).
Match chemical symbols to their elements using a symbol key.

Read given formulae (e.g. H2O, CO2, NaCl) aloud, naming each element and how many atoms of each are present (for NaCl, which is not made of separate molecules, read the formula as a 1:1 ratio of sodium to chlorine).
Decide for each example whether it is an element or a compound and justify it.
activities.intendedInsight: Atoms have internal structure 	a2014 a central nucleus of protons and neutrons with electrons arranged in shells around it 	a2014 and chemical symbols are a shorthand; a formula names the elements present and the number of atoms of each. Detailed electron arrangement is kept light at this stage.

activities.title: Classify and build: check understanding
feedback: Matching and selecting check classification but do not by themselves show a learner can independently construct a formula 	a2014 include a build/fill-in step so learners produce, not just select.

If a learner cannot explain WHY water does not burn (only that it does not), that is a partial response: definitions without the bonding mechanism; prompt them to explain in terms of chemically joined atoms making a new substance.
activities.rationale: Classifying, matching and formula construction assess exactly the targeted outcomes and are best used after the building and properties activities. Including a construction step guards against mistaking recognition for independent production; recognition alone does not elicit production.
sourceClaims: DfE KS3 Chemistry: simple (Dalton) atomic model; differences between atoms, elements and compounds; chemical symbols and formulae
NGSS MS-PS1-1: [curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-PS1-1]
learnerActions: Classify given particle diagrams as element, compound or mixture and justify each choice.
Match chemical symbols to their elements.
Build or complete a formula by filling in how many of each atom for a described molecule.
Transfer to fresh cases: water, carbon dioxide (CO2), sodium chloride (NaCl), and iron sulfide.
activities.intendedInsight: Learners can apply the element/compound/mixture distinction, read and write simple formulae, and transfer the 'new properties / not physically separable' idea to new substances.

constraints: Appropriate for ages 11	a201312 (UK KS3 / US NGSS MS-PS1-1 introductory level).

Keep sub-atomic detail light: the objective names a simple model with a nucleus of protons and neutrons and electrons in shells 	a2014 introduce these, but keep the DETAILED electron-shell arrangement light and defer it to a later stage. Do not label the nuclear picture a 'Dalton' model (Dalton's model has no internal structure).

At this introductory level the element/compound/mixture logic and formulae are fully conveyed with 2D models and physical materials; detailed 3D molecular geometry is reserved for later molecular-shape work.
A static atom diagram and symbol gallery are reference/vocabulary scaffolds 	a2014 they cannot let a learner build formulae or test separability, so pair them with construction activities.
Recognition and matching tasks assess classification but do not elicit independent formula construction; include a build/fill-in step for production.

The 'try to separate' demonstration and sodium+chlorine	a2192salt demo are illustrative mechanisms; equivalent physical atom-model or paper-based construction can serve the same teaching purpose. Any physical enactment of the sodium+chlorine or iron+sulfur reactions requires appropriate safety controls, which the source does not detail.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original source row marks some citations unverified (NGSS MS-PS1-1 and the AAAS/BEST diagnostics claim, verified:false); only the DfE KS3 claim was marked verified. Treat comparative/effectiveness implications cautiously.

The original 'poor fit' claim that an in-role dialogue cannot teach this was softened: dialogue is less suited to constructive building/testing tasks, but this is a narrowly scoped suitability note, not an established universal limit.

Model inconsistency in the source: the pedagogy summary references a 'simple (Dalton) atomic model' (historically a structure-less solid sphere) while the node description and evidence require a 'simple Bohr model' (nucleus with protons/neutrons, electrons in shells). The corrected activities follow the objective, describe the nuclear structure without naming it 'Dalton', and keep detailed arrangement light. Reviewer should confirm the intended model and expected depth.

The sodium+chlorine	a2192salt and iron/sulfur reactions are demonstrations involving hazardous substances; any physical enactment requires appropriate safety controls, which the source does not detail.

assess.poeTask: Predict-Observe-Explain: show iron filings and yellow sulfur powder mixed in a dish. Ask the child to predict — can a magnet still pull the iron out, and will it still look like iron + sulfur? (Yes: it's a mixture.) Then heat a fresh portion to form grey iron sulfide and ask the same. A child conflating mixture and compound predicts the magnet still works. It doesn't — a new compound formed. The pre-observation reasoning is the diagnostic part.
probeDeeper: Sodium is a metal that explodes in water; chlorine is a poison gas. Together they make table salt you eat. How can that be?
Is water a mixture or a compound? How would you get the hydrogen and oxygen back — could you just filter or evaporate?
In the formula CO₂, how many atoms of each element are there, and is it an element or a compound?
If you mixed iron filings and sulfur powder versus heated them into iron sulfide — what's different about the two results?
assess.correctAnswer: No — water does neither; it puts fires out. When elements combine into a COMPOUND, the compound has completely NEW properties, not the properties of the elements it came from. Hydrogen and oxygen are chemically bonded in water and no longer behave as the separate elements. Full marks need 'a compound's properties are new, unlike a mixture where each part keeps its own'.

errorPatterns.pattern: a compound keeps the properties of its elements ('water has oxygen in it so it helps burning')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast a compound (sodium + chlorine → edible salt, though sodium explodes in water and chlorine is poisonous) with a mixture — bonding creates new properties. Reteach compound-vs-mixture at particle level.
errorPatterns.distractor: It would help things burn, because oxygen is part of it.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: predicts water burns or feeds fire because of the hydrogen/oxygen in it

errorPatterns.pattern: compound and mixture are the same thing ('water is just hydrogen mixed with oxygen')
errorPatterns.nextMove: A mixture separates by physical means and keeps each part's properties; a compound needs a chemical reaction to break and has new properties. Draw both at particle level.
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes, because it's really just hydrogen and oxygen mixed together.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: describes H₂O as a mixture that could be un-mixed physically, not a bonded compound

errorPatterns.pattern: an element is a single atom, so 'oxygen' means one O atom
errorPatterns.nextMove: An element is a substance made of ONE kind of atom (many of them); a molecule is atoms joined; read H₂O as 2 H atoms + 1 O atom bonded. Separate the three terms explicitly.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: conflates atom, element and molecule when reading H₂O or O₂

responseLevels.gap: Predicts water burns/feeds fire from its elements; treats compound as a mixture or muddles atom/element/molecule.
responseLevels.full: Explains that a compound has new properties unlike its elements because they are chemically bonded, distinguishes compound from mixture (separation, particle picture), and reads formulae correctly — transferring to fresh cases (NaCl, CO₂, iron sulfide).
responseLevels.partial: Says water doesn't burn and names it a compound, but can't explain that bonding gives NEW properties or reliably distinguish compound from mixture at the particle level — definitions without the mechanism.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Water has the formula H₂O — it's made from hydrogen and oxygen. Hydrogen burns and oxygen is the gas fires need. So would you expect water to burn, or to help things burn? Then the important part: explain why water behaves the way it does, given what it's made of.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The tier-two reason exposes the classic atoms/compounds error: expecting a compound to inherit its elements' properties (and, underneath, confusing a compound with a mixture). A child who thinks water should burn treats H₂O as hydrogen-and-oxygen sitting together; a child who understands compounds says the bonding makes something new.
